Growth trajectories in Black croaker Cheilotrema saturnum have been derived from otolith-based reconstructions of field-captured individuals across the Southern California Bight. The species attains an ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger sciaenids inhabiting nearshore rocky reefs. Length-at-age data indicate that the wet weight at puberty is approximately 255 grams [Wwp = approximately 255 grams], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes. Males and females exhibit similar length-mass relationships, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] based on the diameter of newly spawned pelagic eggs, which measure roughly one millimeter. This diminutive starting mass reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development during the early planktonic phase, a common pattern among sciaenids that broadcast spawn in coastal waters. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that a body size at puberty near 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters] in total length is consistent with a relatively early maturation schedule given the local thermal regime.

At a sustained water temperature of 16.3 °C [T = 16.3 °C], the age at birth from fertilisation to hatching has been recorded at 15 days [ab = 15 days] under controlled laboratory conditions. This incubation period falls within the range reported for other warm-temperate sciaenids and is influenced by the elevated metabolic demand associated with chorionated embryo development. Newly emerged prolarvae are lectithotrophic and rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, which sustain them through the mouth-closed stage until the onset of exogenous feeding approximately one week post-hatching. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 5% [GSI = approximately 5%] at a water temperature of 16.3 °C [T = 16.3 °C] during the pre-spawning period.

Longevity estimates from recaptured tagged individuals in the wild indicate that the maximum lifespan for Black croaker is 20 years [am = 20 years] when assessed at 16.3 °C [T = 16.3 °C], a duration that underscores the species relatively slow pace of life compared to smaller sciaenids. This remarkable lifespan is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 1244 grams [Wwi = 1244 grams], derived from the asymptotic length-weight relationship established for the population. The largest individuals in the sample were aged between 15 and 18 years and exhibited the characteristic somatic plateau expected in long-lived demersal fishes. Senescence appears to be gradual, with reproductive output declining only in the final two to three years of life rather than through a terminal semelparous event. Field surveys indicate that natural mortality in older age classes is primarily driven by predation from large piscivorous fishes, including California sea lions and broadbill swordfish, along with occasional incidental take in gillnet fisheries operating outside marine protected areas.

Pelagic larval ecology in Cheilotrema saturnum is characterised by a brief yolk-sac phase followed by rapid morphological transformation. The transition from the prolarval stage to active exogenous feeding coincides with the depletion of yolk reserves and the functional development of the jaw apparatus and digestive tract. First feeding typically occurs within a few days of mouth opening, after which the growing ichthyoplankton disperses widely via coastal currents before settling into benthic nursery habitats. Juvenile recruitment into nearshore cobble and eelgrass beds occurs several weeks after the larval-juvenile transition, at which point the young-of-year begin exploiting small crustaceans and polychaetes. Growth rates during the first year are comparatively high, with individuals reaching roughly one-third of their adult length before their first winter. This early growth strategy minimises vulnerability to gape-limited predators and enhances overwinter survival, a pattern observed across numerous temperate sciaenid species that inhabit dynamic nearshore environments.

Reproductive output for this species is modulated by an iteroparous strategy in which females spawn multiple times across an extended breeding season. The total length at puberty of 27 centimeters [Lp = 27 centimeters] corresponds to roughly two years of age under average thermal conditions in the Southern California Bight. At an experimental maintenance temperature of 16.3 °C [T = 16.3 °C], the derived lifespan remains 20 years [am = 20 years], confirming the consistency of this estimate under controlled conditions. Mature females produce pelagic eggs that are fertilised externally during broadcast spawning events, with batch fecundity scaling positively with maternal body size. Comparative data from closely related genera within the Sciaenidae indicate that this life-history strategy is typical of species occupying stable, subtropical reef habitats where episodic recruitment pulses rather than single massive reproductive events sustain population persistence over decadal timescales.
